record.title: A game-generation benchmark finds a gap between check pass rates and complete task success
record.summary: An Ant Group-authored arXiv paper introduces GameASG-Bench, a benchmark of 47 browser-native game-generation tasks with predeclared evaluation interfaces, static checks and browser-executed behavioral checks. Across nine agent stacks, the authors report a highest mean L2 check pass rate of 93.2% but a highest strict task success rate of 55.3% (26/47), where strict success requires delivery and every required check to pass. The result shows that high average check rates can coexist with incomplete task compliance in this benchmark. Each task-configuration pair was run once; these paper-reported results do not establish performance across broader software tasks or independent replication.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The arXiv v1 paper and linked public repository define GameASG-Bench as 47 browser-native game-generation tasks with a predeclared evaluation interface, 336 static L1 checks and 885 browser-executed L2 checks; the authors report that each reference implementation passed all L1 and applicable L2 prerequisite/core checks.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across nine agent stacks on the 47 tasks, the authors report a highest mean L2 check pass rate of 93.2% and a highest strict task success rate of 55.3% (26/47). Strict task success requires valid delivery, completed evaluation and passing all L1 checks and applicable L2 prerequisite and core checks.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the paper's DeepSeek-V4-Flash comparisons, full tool access yields 18 strict task successes versus 6–9 with limited tool access, and the rate over all planned tasks rises from 7/47 to 18/47 as the nominal turn budget increases from 30 to 120. These are single-run benchmark results, not estimates of run-to-run variance.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The benchmark does not establish general autonomous software-generation success outside its browser-game task set, nor does one run per task-configuration establish variance or independent replication.

evidence_gaps.description: The benchmark results have not been independently reproduced. The paper says each task-configuration pair was run once, so run-to-run variation is not estimated.
The evidence is limited to 47 self-contained browser-native game tasks, the tested models/harnesses and the authors' evaluation interface; transfer to general software generation remains unknown.

brief.importance_rationale: If the gap generalizes, agent evaluations based on average check rates can substantially overstate completion of all specified requirements, changing how autonomous software systems are evaluated and deployed. Consequence is notable within software-agent evaluation, while evidence is one benchmark and single-run configurations.
limitations: The primary evidence is an author-reported arXiv v1 paper and linked author repository; no independent replication was performed in this review.
The 47 tasks are browser-native games with self-contained index.html delivery, not a representative sample of software engineering tasks.
Each task-configuration pair is run once, so the study does not estimate run-to-run variance.

The strict-success and check-pass metrics differ by construction: strict success requires every check to pass, while mean check rates aggregate partial compliance. Their gap is informative but not a direct general measure of agent capability.
brief.summary: An Ant Group-authored arXiv paper introduces GameASG-Bench, a benchmark of 47 browser-native game-generation tasks with predeclared evaluation interfaces, static checks and browser-executed behavioral checks. Across nine agent stacks, the authors report a highest mean L2 check pass rate of 93.2% but a highest strict task success rate of 55.3% (26/47), where strict success requires delivery and every required check to pass. The result shows that high average check rates can coexist with incomplete task compliance in this benchmark. technical.claimed_result: The paper reports a 93.2% highest mean L2 check-pass rate and 55.3% highest strict task success across nine agent stacks on 47 browser-game tasks; the highest strict success is 26/47.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports token use and monetary cost for the tested stacks. The review did not independently recalculate costs or execute the benchmark.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper and public repository specify the benchmark tasks, evaluation interface and metrics. Reported agent outcomes remain author-reported and unreproduced in this review.
technical.implementation_status: The authors publish task materials and a Docker-based runner. The repository was inspected but not executed.
technical.mechanism: Task authors define legal scenarios, player-level actions, stable state observations and invariants before generation. L1 checks inspect source compliance; L2 checks run browser interactions and inspect runtime evidence. Strict task success requires delivery and every applicable prerequisite/core check to pass.
technical.novelty: Makes behavioral testability part of requirement-to-artifact generation and distinguishes average check completion from all-required-check task success.
technical.regime: 47 self-contained browser-native game tasks across 12 genres, 2D and 3D, nine tested model/harness stacks and one run per task-configuration pair.
technical.reproducibility: Public author repository and task/evaluation materials are available. No code was run and no independent reproduction was established.
technical.strongest_baseline: Nine tested model/harness stacks use the same 47 task packages and evaluation protocol; within-stack tool-access, turn-budget, reasoning-effort and harness comparisons are reported.

brief.title: A game-generation benchmark finds a gap between check pass rates and complete task success
brief.why_it_matters: If the gap generalizes, average pass rates can make agent-generated software appear more complete than it is under all specified requirements. The benchmark makes that distinction measurable, but its single-run browser-game results need replication and transfer tests before broader conclusions.
